newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan president sacks Bhutto, sets poll date.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan president sacks Bhutto, sets poll date.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari sacked Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto and her cabinet on Tuesday, dissolved parliament and announced new elections for February 3.
The president's move, reported by the official news agency APP, cut short Bhutto's three-year-old government as she struggled against mounting political and economic storms.
Leghari named Meraj Khalid, a former Speaker of the National Assembly, as interim prime minister, APP said, quoting unofficial reports.

"I am satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the Federation cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and an appeal to the electorate is necessary," said the president's proclamation.

"Now therefore, in exercise of my powers under Article 58(2)(b) of the Constitution, I Farooq Ahmad Khan Leghari, President of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, hereby dissolve the National Assembly with immediate effect and the Prime Minister and her Cabinet shall cease to hold office forthwith.

"Further, in exercise of my powers under Article 48(5) of the Constitution I hereby appoint 3rd February 1997 as the date on which general elections shall be held to the National Assembly," the proclamation said.
Bhutto has been in power since general elections in October 1993. The president has constitutional powers to dismiss elected governments and dissolve parliament's lower house.
Bhutto's spokesman Farhatullah Babar said Bhutto had received a letter from the president between 1.30 and 1.45 a.m. (2130 and 2145 GMT) at her official residence in Islamabad.
"She is at her house but is not receiving any calls at the moment," he told Reuters by telephone. He said he expected Bhutto to react publicly later in the day, but gave no details.
Asked if there had been any military deployment, he said: "No, no such thing."
Witnesses said some army trucks were moving in the streets of Islamabad. Mobile telephone services were disconnected.
Bhutto has portrayed herself abroad as a woman struggling against the odds to steer her turbulent Islamic country on a moderate course of economic liberalisation and social justice.
Her critics at home flay her for leading what they say is a corrupt, inept government that has fumbled its foreign policy, flirted with economic ruin and trampled on human rights.
Bhutto's troubles have proliferated in the past two months.
Police in the violence-prone city of Karachi shot dead her estranged brother Murtaza and seven of his men on September 20 in circumstances now being investigated by a judicial inquiry.

Lawyers for Ghinwa Bhutto, Murtaza's widow, have accused Bhutto's husband Asif Ali Zardari, Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar and Sindh Province Chief Minister Abdullah Shah of conspiring to kill the prime minister's flamboyant brother. The three men deny the charge.

Last month a strike called by the main opposition party led by Nawaz Sharif was followed by more dramatic anti-corruption protests by the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party that police in Islamabad and nearby Rawalpindi quelled with teargas and batons.

In the latest crisis, the Lahore High Court reinstated Manzoor Wattoo as chief minister of Punjab province on Sunday, saying that his dismissal last year, by presidential proclamation on Bhutto's recommendation, had been unlawful.
